clue.text: Police for the Archbishop?

blocks.note: first meaning: London's force, known in full by this adjective plus Police
second meaning: an archbishop presiding over a church province

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for some clerical police force; in fact one word describes both London's police and an archbishop who heads a province.
explanation.definitionFit: London's force is officially the Metropolitan Police, and an archbishop ruling a province of bishops is called a metropolitan.

clue.text: Target set perhaps, for sales outlets

indicators.note: perhaps says the word might be arranged otherwise, so its letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: a mark is something aimed at
the three letters reordered

explanation.surface: A sales target is fixed for the shops.
explanation.walkthrough: Target set reads as a business goal; it splits into a target and a jumbled word.
explanation.definitionFit: Markets are places where goods are sold, stalls and outlets for traders' wares.

clue.text: Mainly controlled by gravity of satellite situation

definitions.text: Mainly controlled by gravity of satellite situation

blocks.clueFragment: Mainly controlled by gravity of satellite
blocks.note: the surface reading: a space probe's orbit governed chiefly by gravity
the setter's reading: the condition of the main, the sea, pulled by the Moon

explanation.walkthrough: Mainly hides the main, an old word for the sea, and the satellite is the Moon, whose pull raises the waters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidal state is one of the sea rising and falling under the Moon's gravitational attraction.

clue.text: Omission of periscope's function

blocks.note: first meaning: a mistake of leaving something out
second meaning, read literally: sight over the top of an obstacle

explanation.surface: A submarine's report blames a failure on its periscope's use.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: a periscope gives sight over a barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: An oversight is a careless failure to notice or include something, a slip of attention.

clue.text: River offers no employment

blocks.note: O looks like a zero, nothing
employment of something is its use

explanation.surface: A river town provides no jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Employment looks like jobs, but it is the act of using something. The Ouse is a river in England, the name of several.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ouse is a well-known English river, flowing through York among other places.

clue.text: Being jagged, is put in order

blocks.note: first meaning: notched along an edge
second meaning: ordered as goods by a requisition form

explanation.surface: Something rough-edged is being tidied up.
explanation.walkthrough: Put in order looks like tidied, but it means requisitioned: to indent for supplies is to place an official order.
explanation.definitionFit: An indented coastline is notched, and goods indented for have been formally requested on an order form.

clue.text: Currently charged with a vile fabrication

indicators.note: a fabrication is something made up, so the letters are built into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is now accused on the strength of a nasty lie.
explanation.walkthrough: Currently charged sounds legal, but it is electrical: a wire carrying current.
explanation.definitionFit: An alive wire is a live one, carrying electric current, so it is electrically charged.

clue.text: Palmist's vade-mecum?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a pocket reference guide
the setter's reading: the guide a palm reader works from is the human palm, so a book of hands

explanation.walkthrough: A vade-mecum is a reference book carried for ready use; for a palmist the material read is the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A handbook is a compact guide or manual, exactly what a vade-mecum is.

clue.text: Pact made half this way into Death Valley

definitions.text: half this way into Death Valley

blocks.note: first meaning: an alliance or agreement

blocks.clueFragment: half this way into Death Valley
blocks.note: second meaning: Tennyson's Charge of the Light Brigade rides half of this distance onward into the valley of Death

explanation.surface: An agreement struck halfway along a route into the California desert.
explanation.walkthrough: Death Valley looks like the American desert, but it is Tennyson's valley of Death; the poem opens 'Half a league, half a league'. A league is about three miles.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is an alliance bound by agreement, and also an old measure of distance of around three miles.

clue.text: Changed gear, having made readjustment

blocks.note: first meaning: put on clothes again, gear being clothing
second meaning: put right, restored the balance

explanation.surface: A driver shifts gear while making a correction to the car.
explanation.walkthrough: Gear sounds mechanical, but here it is clothing: someone who dressed again has re-dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Re-dressed is clothed afresh, and redressed means set right a wrong or restored an imbalance.

clue.text: Statue of one Balthazar?

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
Balthazar is traditionally one of the three Magi, the wise men

explanation.surface: A question about a statue depicting Balthazar, the wise man of the Nativity.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Balthazar is an example of a magus, singular mage.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a carved likeness, and image in older usage means an idol or sculpted figure.

clue.text: Join up cracked tiles round new opening

indicators.note: cracked things are broken apart, so the letters are rearranged
an opening is the start, so only the first letter of the word is kept
going round something encloses it, so one part sits inside the other

blocks.note: the five letters reordered
the first letter of new; N is also the usual abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A roofer fixes broken tiles around a new hole in the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged tiles wrap round N after the first letter, giving E-N-LIST.
explanation.definitionFit: To join up is to sign on for the armed forces, which is to enlist.

clue.text: He's likely to lose a lower canine

blocks.note: first meaning: the competitor not expected to win
second meaning, read literally: a dog that is beneath another

explanation.surface: A dentist warns a patient that a bottom eye-tooth may fall out.
explanation.walkthrough: Canine looks like a tooth, but it is a dog; a dog placed lower is an under-dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The underdog is the contestant expected to be beaten, originally the dog pinned beneath in a fight.

clue.text: Missile-launchers for supporting arms

blocks.note: first meaning: weapons that hurl stones, as David used
second meaning: fabric loops that hold up an injured arm

explanation.surface: An arms dealer lists rocket launchers suited to back up an army's weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Arms in the surface are weapons; in the second meaning they are limbs held in a support.
explanation.definitionFit: A sling is both a strap weapon for throwing stones and a bandage loop that cradles a hurt limb.

clue.text: Clive as trader ?

blocks.note: the surface reading: Robert Clive, Clive of India, who began as a clerk for the East India Company
the setter's reading: a merchant ship sailing to India

explanation.walkthrough: Clive of India was literally a man of India, but the word is a large trading ship of the East India Company.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indiaman was a large merchant sailing vessel trading with India and the East Indies.

clue.text: By no means rare words of praise

blocks.note: first meaning: of steak, cooked right through
second meaning: an exclamation congratulating someone

explanation.surface: Praise that is far from uncommon.
explanation.walkthrough: Rare reads as scarce, but it is the steak sense: lightly cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Steak cooked thoroughly is the opposite of rare, and the same phrase congratulates someone on a fine effort.

clue.text: Gulliver would appear humiliated to Brobdingnag

blocks.note: the setter's reading: seem ashamed or belittled

blocks.clueFragment: Gulliver would appear humiliated to Brobdingnag
blocks.note: the surface reading: in Brobdingnag, the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels, the hero seems tiny

explanation.walkthrough: Brobdingnag is the giants' country in Gulliver's Travels, where Gulliver literally seems tiny; the phrase also means seem humbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To look small is an idiom for appearing foolish or humbled before others, so it means seem humiliated.

clue.text: Is successfully removed

blocks.note: the surface reading: something detached without trouble
the setter's reading: a phrasal verb that also means succeeds, as a plan does

explanation.walkthrough: The phrasal verb means both detaches and works out well, so the clue blends the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A lid that detaches cleanly has come off, and a plan that succeeds also comes off.

clue.text: Insurrection (not as published up north)

blocks.note: the plain definition: incitement to rebel against the state
a teasing aside: written with a full stop after its first letter, the word would look like the Scottish printing of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style entry with a note that northern editions print it differently.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket teases that the word looks like S(cottish) edition, the version of a paper printed up north, and assures us it is not that.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedition is conduct or speech stirring people to rise against lawful authority, close kin to insurrection.

clue.text: It's a complex method

blocks.note: first meaning: a network of interlinked parts
second meaning: an orderly procedure

explanation.surface: A remark that some procedure is complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: Complex reads as an adjective, but here it is a noun, a whole made of connected parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is an organised set of connected things and also a planned way of doing something.

clue.text: Had pay cut in harbour

blocks.note: first meaning: had money deducted from wages
second meaning: tied up at a quay

explanation.surface: A sailor had wages reduced while the ship sat in port.
explanation.definitionFit: Docked wages are reduced ones, and a docked ship is moored at a berth in port.

clue.text: Extraction of French perfume

blocks.note: de is French for of
a scent is a perfume

explanation.surface: The process of drawing out the essence of a French fragrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Extraction suggests distilling perfume, but it means ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone of Irish extraction is of Irish lineage, and descent likewise means ancestry or origin.

clue.text: Having a keen edge to one's appetite

definitions.text: Having a keen edge to one's appetite

blocks.note: the surface reading: a blade honed until sharp
the setter's reading: very hungry

explanation.walkthrough: Keen edge sounds like a knife, but the phrase describes hunger; the same compound once meant a blade set sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp-set is an old adjective for ravenous, eager for food, with the keenness of a whetted blade.

clue.text: A problem for the model

blocks.note: first meaning: a puzzling question
second meaning: one who poses, for a painter or camera

explanation.surface: A difficulty facing a fashion model.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is a baffling question, and also someone who strikes poses, as an artist's sitter does.

clue.text: Guess a change is needed in customs

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller is told to guess, since some change is called for at customs.
explanation.walkthrough: Customs looks like the border post, but here it means habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Usages are established practices or habits, the same as customs in the sense of traditions.

clue.text: Condition, of course, important in race issues

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the state of the ground on a racecourse
the surface reading: a matter that weighs in racial questions, really a factor in horse races

explanation.walkthrough: Of course reads as naturally, but it is of the racecourse; race issues suggests politics but means the results of horse races.
explanation.definitionFit: In horse racing the going describes how firm or soft the turf is, which affects which runners do well.

clue.text: The case for designing an upper-class tie

indicators.note: designing means shaping into a new pattern, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for upper-class
taken as written

explanation.surface: An argument in favour of creating a smart necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: The case reads as an argument; it is a small container. U for upper-class was popularised by Nancy Mitford.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental container for needles, scissors or cosmetics, a crossword favourite.

clue.text: Sex-mad art master taken back in for tests

indicators.note: something mad is crazy and disordered, so the letters are jumbled
taking something back returns it the way it came, so it is read backwards
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the three letters rearranged
MA is Master of Arts

explanation.surface: A lecherous art teacher is taken back on for the testing season.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled letters are split by the reversed degree: EX-AM-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Exams are formal examinations, the written or practical tests students sit.

clue.text: Pan one's found in East German nation

indicators.note: something found in another is located inside it

blocks.note: Ost is German for east
a people or nation
one is I, and 's is is

explanation.surface: Someone's cooking pan turns up somewhere in East Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: East German means the German for east, not a citizen of the old GDR. One's is I plus is.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan someone is to criticise harshly, and ostracise means to exclude or condemn by common consent; a loose fit.

clue.text: Unusual Bank Holiday report on "Crossroads"?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a road news bulletin saying the roads are quiet, rare on a public holiday
the setter's reading: the signal posted at a road junction

explanation.surface: A rare piece of holiday news about the TV soap Crossroads.
explanation.walkthrough: On a Bank Holiday, a British public holiday, roads are jammed, so a report of light traffic would be unusual. Crossroads was a British TV soap set in a motel.
explanation.definitionFit: Signals of red, amber and green stand at junctions to control vehicles, so they are the lights at crossroads.
